1. Scientific Analysis

Analysis Type

AFM peptide self-assembly: physical-height mapping, plane+row-median+destripe leveling, square resampling, scan-line FFT masking, targeted Fourier reflection mapping (3-10 nm band)

Interpretation

The raw AFM height map is dominated by a large low-frequency tilt/bow (RMS = 14.28 nm across a ~400 x 400 nm field), which is instrumental in origin (sample tilt plus scanner bow) rather than a real topographic feature. Plane fitting removes essentially all of this (RMS drops to 0.244 nm), and the additional row-median + per-column polynomial destripe brings the residual roughness down to Rq = 0.203 nm — sub-Angstrom-to-atomic-step scale corrugation. The leveled residual and square-resampled panels reveal the true structure: broad, flat terrace-like domains with sharp, straight edges oriented diagonally, consistent with layered/terraced material (the MoS2 substrate and/or peptide film patches) rather than a molecularly periodic lattice. The FFT log-power shows a strong diagonal power lobe and a cross of scan-line streaks, but no discrete reciprocal-lattice spots in the targeted 3-10 nm band. The single candidate reflection is weak (1.81 sigma, below significance) and the detected vertical feature at 0.0058 cyc/px (~134 nm period) is far outside any molecular self-assembly range — it is a slow scan-line/drift artifact and is correctly excluded. The diagonal FFT lobes correspond to residual diagonal streaks noted as a known leveling limitation, i.e., instrumental line-to-line correlation rather than a periodic monolayer motif. Net physical picture: the imaged surface consists of smooth, low-roughness terraced domains with no measurable in-plane periodic self-assembled peptide lattice at the resolution and length scales probed.

3. Scientific Claims

Claim 1: No resolvable periodic peptide self-assembly is detected in the 3-10 nm band; the only Fourier candidate is statistically insignificant (1.81 sigma) and the sub-Angstrom residual roughness (Rq = 0.20 nm) reflects smooth terraced domains rather than an ordered lattice.

Scientific Impact: Indicates that under these conditions the MoS2-binding peptide does not form a laterally ordered (crystalline/periodic) monolayer detectable by AFM, suggesting adsorption in a disordered, amorphous, or sub-resolution conformal film — an important negative constraint for engineering ordered biomolecular templates on 2D materials.

Literature Search Query: Has anyone observed the absence of long-range periodic ordering in MoS2-binding peptide films self-assembled on MoS2 as measured by AFM Fourier analysis?

Keywords: MoS2-binding peptide, self-assembly, AFM, Fourier analysis, surface ordering

4. Caveats & Limitations

The absence of a detectable period is resolution- and scale-limited: at 0.783 nm/px square sampling, sub-nm molecular repeats (e.g., peptide backbone spacings) are below Nyquist and could not be seen even if present. Residual diagonal streaks persist after leveling and produce the FFT diagonal lobes, meaning weak true periodicity could be masked by, or confused with, instrumental line correlation. The ~134 nm 'period' is a scan artifact, not sample structure. The single weak reflection (1.81 sigma) is below significance, so the negative result is a non-detection, not proof of complete disorder.
